newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Asia says Hanson hurting Australian trade. [CORRECTED 07:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Asia says Hanson hurting Australian trade. [CORRECTED 07:55 GMT]

text.p: Asian business leaders say Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson is damaging Australia-Asia trade and is more recognisable than the country's prime minister, according to a newspaper poll on Monday.

The Sydney Morning Herald poll, which surveyed 200 business leaders in Kuala Lumpur, Manila, Bangkok and Jakarta, found that six to seven percent (corrects from 16 percent) were now less likely to do business with Australian companies.
The poll also found that 25 percent had heard of Hanson, while only five percent had heard of Prime Minister John Howard.
Hanson's name was recognised by 76 percent of respondents in Kuala Lumpur, 28 percent in Jakarta, 26 percent in Bangkok and 16 percent in Manila.
One comment from Kuala Lumpur said: "She is damaging for prospective Asians planning on going to Australia. The racist problem now makes people think twice about going there".

One Manila respondent said Hanson did not want to do business with Asia and that she should not be "closing doors to her neighbours like this". A Bangkok respondent said she was anti-Asian and did not like Asian immigration.

But the survey found that 84 percent of business leaders thought Australia was a "favourable" or "very favourable" country with which to do business, while 88 percent thought it was a "favourable" or "very favourable" holiday destination.
Independent politician Hanson sparked a bitter race debate in Australia last September when she made her maiden speech to parliament, claiming Australia was being swamped by Asians.
Hanson's newly-registered One Nation party, which has a platform of anti-immigration and anti-Aborginal welfare, has attracted rowdy, and and at times, violent protests.
Opinion polls show support for Hanson in Australia ranging between six and 10 percent.
